sections.h2: Can my meter handle another AC?
p: The meter itself only records units; what limits you is the sanctioned load in kW on your bill, the main breaker at the meter and the service cable into the house. Add the AC's running watts to the connected load, take the share expected to run at once (0.6 for a home) and round up to a whole kW. In the default case 1,500 W plus a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter makes 2,950 W, an expected demand of 1.77 kW, so it needs 2 kW: on 2 kW it is within the sanctioned load.

On a 1 kW connection the same home needs a higher sanctioned load first, at least 2 kW, and on 5 kW it uses 35% with 3.23 kW of headroom, so the answer depends on the sanctioned load far more than on the meter. Also check that the main breaker rating is above the new current of 16 A.

sections.h2: How do I add an AC to my house load?
p: First find the connected load: add up the running watts of every appliance in the house with the home load calculator, or from their labels. Then pick the AC. The calculator adds the AC's running watts, which is the right number for the check because on a hot afternoon an inverter AC runs near its rated input for long stretches; its lower average draw is for the electricity bill, not for the load.

The result shows the new total in watts and amps, how much of the sanctioned load it uses, and the MCB rating for the AC's own circuit. If you plan a second AC, run the calculator again with the first result as the connected load.

sections.h2: What sanctioned load do I need for an AC?
p: The sanctioned load must cover the expected demand, the new total × 0.6, rounded up to a whole kW; the sanctioned load calculator uses the same rule. With 1,500 W of other load and a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter the new total is 2.95 kW and the demand 1.77 kW, so 2 kW is the minimum to apply for. A small home with 800 W of fans, lights and a fridge can add a Split AC 1 ton inverter on 2 kW at 51%.

Apply for a little more than the minimum if you expect to add appliances, but remember the fixed charge on the bill is per sanctioned kW, and that 5 kW or more puts the connection on the time-of-use tariff.

sections.h2: What is the AC load on a single phase supply in amps?
p: An AC's own current is its running watts ÷ (volts × its own power factor, about 0.9 for an inverter AC and 0.8 for a non-inverter). At 230 V a Split AC 1 ton inverter draws about 4.3 A, a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter about 7 A and a Split AC 1.5 ton non-inverter about 9.8 A while running.

The non-inverter compressor is the one to watch: its start surge of 5,400 W pushes the whole house to 40.2 A for a moment in the example below, which is what trips a main breaker that is already near its rating.

sections.h2: What home wiring does a new AC need?
p: A dedicated circuit from the distribution board: its own copper cable of at least 2.5 mm² (7/29 in Pakistani sizes), its own MCB and a proper earth. Never run an AC from a socket circuit shared with other appliances. For a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter that is a 16 A type C MCB on 2.5 mm² (7/29) cable; the AC wire size page sizes the cable and breaker at the AC's maximum input with a safety margin and checks the voltage drop over your cable run, so use that for the final sizes.
If the house is older and the main cable or distribution board is already warm or discoloured, have an electrician check it before adding the AC, whatever this calculator says.

sections.h2: Can my meter take two ACs?
p: Run the check twice. The 1,500 W home above reaches 2,950 W with the first Split AC 1.5 ton inverter; a second one on top takes it to 4,400 W and 23.9 A, an expected demand of 2.64 kW. Two 1.5 ton ACs plus normal household load therefore need a 3 kW sanctioned load, and each AC needs its own circuit and MCB.

faq.q: Can my meter handle a 1.5 ton AC?
faq.a: If the expected demand, (the connected load + the AC's 1,450 W) × 0.6 rounded up to a whole kW, stays within the sanctioned kW on your bill and the main breaker rating, yes. With 1,500 W already connected it needs 2 kW: on 1 kW it needs a higher sanctioned load first, at least 2 kW, and on 5 kW it fits at 35%.

faq.q: What sanctioned load is needed for two ACs?
faq.a: Two 1.5 ton inverter ACs with normal household load come to about 4,400 W connected and 2.64 kW of expected demand, so 3 kW is the minimum sanctioned load, below the 5 kW at which a connection moves to time-of-use billing.

faq.q: Does an inverter AC need less sanctioned load than a non-inverter?
faq.a: A little: a 1.5 ton inverter runs at about 1,450 W against 1,800 W for a non-inverter, and it has no start surge, while the non-inverter draws 5,400 W for a moment at every start. The inverter is also much cheaper to run.

faq.q: Can I run an AC on a 1 kW connection?
faq.a: A Split AC 1.5 ton inverter alone is 1,450 W running, already above 1 kW, so no. A Split AC 1 ton inverter at 900 W leaves almost nothing for fans and lights. Apply for a higher sanctioned load first.

faq.q: What size breaker and wire does the AC circuit need?
faq.a: A Split AC 1.5 ton inverter is designed at 1,900 W, its maximum input, which is 9.2 A; with the motor margin that needs a 16 A type C MCB on 2.5 mm² (7/29) copper cable. The AC wire size page uses the same rule and also checks your cable length.

faq.q: Will adding an AC change my tariff slab?
faq.a: The slab depends on units used, not on load. An AC adds units every month it runs and can push the whole bill into a higher slab; the AC units calculator shows how many units and rupees to expect.

faq.q: Does the main breaker need to change for the new AC?
faq.a: Only if the new current is close to its rating: the default home draws 16 A with the AC on and 18.5 A at full speed. An electrician should confirm the main breaker and service cable rating before the AC is connected.

key_facts: A Split AC 1.5 ton inverter adds about 1,450 W of running load and up to 1,900 W at full speed; a non-inverter AC of the same size adds a starting surge of about three times its running watts for a second or two.
Current with everything on after adding an AC = (connected load + the AC's running watts) ÷ (volts × power factor): the default home goes from 8.2 A to 16 A at 230 V.

The sanctioned load a home needs is its connected load × 0.6 diversity, rounded up to a whole kW, the same rule as the sanctioned load calculator; if that is above the kW on the bill, apply to the DISCO for a higher sanctioned load before the AC is installed. At 5 kW or more a domestic connection moves to time-of-use billing.

Every AC needs its own circuit from the distribution board, with a copper cable of at least 2.5 mm² (7/29) and its own MCB; a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter needs a 16 A type C MCB on 2.5 mm² (7/29) cable, sized at the AC's maximum input with a safety margin; the AC wire size page also checks your cable length.
mistakes: Using the AC's average draw for the check. The average is for the bill; for the load use the running watts, because on a hot afternoon an inverter AC runs near its rated input for long periods.
Forgetting the non-inverter start surge. A Split AC 1.5 ton non-inverter draws 5,400 W for a moment at every compressor start, several times its 1,800 W running load.
Running the new AC from an existing socket circuit. An AC needs its own cable and MCB from the distribution board; a shared circuit already carrying other loads will overheat or trip.

Ignoring the sanctioned load because the meter does not trip. The DISCO can raise the sanctioned load and fixed charges after a load survey, and a service cable running above its rating is a fire risk.

how.text: 1,500 W connected now + 1,450 W for the Split AC 1.5 ton inverter = 2,950 W. 2,950 W ÷ (230 V × 0.8 power factor) = 16 A, up from 8.2 A today. Expected demand = 2.95 kW × 0.6 diversity (not everything runs at once) = 1.77 kW, rounded up to a whole kW = 2 kW of sanctioned load, the same rule as the sanctioned load calculator; on 2 kW the home is within the sanctioned load (89% of it). For a moment at compressor start or full speed the load is 1,500 W + 1,900 W = 3,400 W (18.5 A). The AC's own circuit is designed at the AC's maximum input: 1,900 W ÷ (230 V × 0.9, the AC's own power factor) = 9.2 A; with the margin a compressor load gets, the next standard MCB is 16 A type C on a cable rated at least 16 A: 2.5 mm², rated 19 A in 45 °C air, the same as on the AC wire size page.

legal.t: This is an estimate, not an official bill. Your DISCO's bill and NEPRA's tariff notifications are the official figures. Do not use this result as evidence before a court, NEPRA, the Wafaqi Mohtasib or any other forum. To dispute a bill, complain to your DISCO first, using the complaint number printed on your bill, then file a NEPRA complaint or a Wafaqi Mohtasib complaint.

examples.title: 1,500 W home adds a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter on a 1 kW connection
examples.text: 1,500 W + 1,450 W = 2,950 W, or 16 A. The expected demand of 1.77 kW is 177% of the 1 kW sanctioned load, so this connection needs a higher sanctioned load first, at least 2 kW. The AC's own circuit needs a 16 A type C MCB on 2.5 mm² cable.

examples.title: The same AC on a 5 kW connection
examples.text: 1,500 W + 1,450 W = 2,950 W, or 16 A, an expected demand of 1.77 kW: 35% of 5 kW with 3.23 kW of headroom. This connection can take the AC and still has room for another one.

examples.title: Small home adds a Split AC 1 ton inverter
examples.text: 800 W of fans, lights and a fridge + 900 W = 1,700 W, or 9.2 A. The expected demand of 1.02 kW is 51% of a 2 kW sanctioned load, so it fits with 0.98 kW to spare. The AC circuit needs a 10 A type C MCB on a cable rated at least 10 A: 2.5 mm², rated 19 A in 45 °C air, the same as on the AC wire size page.

examples.title: Split AC 1.5 ton non-inverter on a 2 kW connection
examples.text: 2,000 W + 1,800 W = 3,800 W, or 20.7 A, an expected demand of 2.28 kW: this 2 kW connection needs a higher sanctioned load first, at least 3 kW. Worse, the compressor start of 5,400 W pushes the peak to 7,400 W, or 40.2 A for a moment. An inverter AC or a higher sanctioned load is the fix.

examples.title: Second Split AC 1.5 ton inverter in a home that already runs one
examples.text: 2,950 W including the first AC + 1,450 W = 4,400 W, or 23.9 A, an expected demand of 2.64 kW. That needs 3 kW of sanctioned load, so two ACs fit on 3 kW at 88% with 0.36 kW left.

content.answer: Adding a Split AC 1.5 ton inverter (1,450 W running) to a home with 1,500 W gives a new total of 2,950 W, or 16 A at 230 V. Not everything runs at once, so the expected demand is 2.95 kW × 0.6 = 1.77 kW, which needs a 2 kW sanctioned load: this home on 2 kW is within the sanctioned load. New total = current watts + the AC's running watts.

formula.text: P_new = P_now + P_ac; I = P_new ÷ (V × PF); sanctioned kW needed = ceil(P_new ÷ 1000 × diversity)
lines: P_now = connected load today (every appliance installed, running watts)
P_ac = the AC's running watts (its starting watts give the momentary peak)
I = current in amps, V = supply voltage, PF = power factor
diversity = the share of the connected load expected to run at once (home default, as on the sanctioned load calculator); load % = expected demand ÷ sanctioned kW

AC circuit: I_ac = P_ac,max ÷ (V × PF_ac) with P_ac,max = the AC's maximum input; MCB = next standard size ≥ I_ac × margin (compressor load); cable rated (after the air-temperature correction) ≥ the MCB and ≥ I_ac × margin

content.safety: An AC must be on its own circuit with a correctly sized cable, MCB and earth; have a licensed electrician install it and check the main breaker and service cable before you add the load.
